texts.title: The Second Reading
texts.author: Manuel Academy
texts.source: Authored for Manuel Academy High School ELA; Academy-held rights.
texts.summary: A student re-reads a letter they thought they understood and finds the second reading contradicts the first. Written to make 'strong and thorough evidence' a felt problem rather than a definition.
texts.opening_passage: The letter had been on the counter for three days before Nadia read it properly. The first time, she had read it the way you read a sign in a language you half know - catching the shape of it, filling the rest in from what she expected it to say.

texts.title: Two Clocks
texts.author: Manuel Academy
texts.source: Authored for Manuel Academy High School ELA; Academy-held rights.
texts.summary: A narrative told on two timelines that converge, built so that pacing and flashback are analyzable at the sentence level.
texts.opening_passage: At 6:14 the kitchen was still dark. Eleven years earlier, at 6:14, it had been the brightest room in a different house.

texts.title: The Ordinance Nobody Read
texts.author: Manuel Academy
texts.source: Authored for Manuel Academy High School ELA; Academy-held rights.
texts.summary: A local-government argument with a deliberately planted unsupported inference and one genuinely sufficient evidence chain, for validity-versus-sufficiency work.
texts.opening_passage: Supporters of the ordinance say the intersection is dangerous. The record shows eleven collisions in four years. Whether eleven is many depends on a comparison the sponsors have not made.

texts.title: Field Notes on a Retreating Shore
texts.author: Manuel Academy
texts.source: Authored for Manuel Academy High School ELA; Academy-held rights.
texts.summary: An explanatory article with headings and a data figure, written as a model for W.2 organization and graphics that genuinely aid comprehension.
texts.opening_passage: The shoreline moves every year. What changed recently is not the movement but our ability to measure it at the scale of a single season.

texts.title: The Gettysburg Address
texts.author: Abraham Lincoln
texts.source: U.S. National Archives (federal government work, public domain)
texts.summary: 272 words; a compact object for cumulative diction and structural analysis.

texts.title: Declaration of Sentiments (Seneca Falls)
texts.author: Elizabeth Cady Stanton and the Seneca Falls Convention
texts.summary: Deliberately modeled on the Declaration of Independence; a clean case for source transformation.

texts.title: The Story of an Hour
texts.author: Kate Chopin
texts.summary: Short enough to read whole in one session; irony and structural reversal are unmissable.

texts.title: Ozymandias
texts.author: Percy Bysshe Shelley
texts.summary: Frame-within-frame point of view in fourteen lines.

texts.title: The Iliad (Butler translation), Book I
texts.author: Homer, tr. Samuel Butler
texts.summary: Public-domain translation; supports world-literature point of view (9-10.RL.6).

texts.title: Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass, Chapters I-VII
texts.author: Frederick Douglass
texts.summary: Rhetorical purpose and evidence in a first-person account.

texts.title: A Modest Proposal
texts.author: Jonathan Swift
texts.summary: Satire that fails safely when read literally, so the gap between stated and meant is teachable.

texts.title: Letter from Birmingham Jail
texts.author: Martin Luther King Jr.
texts.source: Named as an example in the Michigan ELA standards. Text is NOT included in this package.
